newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 15.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- INFLATION SETBACK FOR CLARKE

Figures from the National Office of Statistics reveal that the underlying rate in inflation in the UK rose to 3.3 per cent last month from 2.9 per cent in September. The unexpected surge has fuelled expectations of a further increase in interest rates, although both the prime minister John Major and his chancellor Kenneth Clarke have sought to play down the rise, claiming it is a statistical aberration caused by an exceptionally low rate for the same month last year.
-- GUS BUYS US CREDIT RATING AGENCY FOR 1.04 BILLION STG

British-based retail group Great Universal Stores has acquired the US credit rating and information agency Experian in a 1.04 billion stg deal. The surprise move prompted a rise in GUS shares of 58.5p to close Thursday at 648p. GUS, which operates a mail order empire as well as owning the Burberry luxury goods label, will merge Experian with its own credit rating and information group, CNN.
-- GAPS IN PAY STOP WIDENING FOR FIRST TIME IN 15 YEARS

The latest edition of government statistics on Households Below Average Income reveals that inequalities of income in the UK have stopped widening for the first time in 15 years. The figures appear to show a pause in the trend towards the rich getting richer and the poor poorer, with the share of total income taken by the top 10 per cent of the population remaining static at 26 per cent (after housing costs) and the share taken by the bottom 10 per cent also static at 2.5 per cent.
-- BIRT LOSES BATTLE FOR LICENCE FEE RISE ABOVE INFLATION

The department of national heritage is said to be close to announcing a five-year deal for the funding of the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) which will see the value of the licence fee paid by all television users remain static in real terms. The deal will disappoint BBC director-general John Birt, who has campaigned for a licence fee increase greater than the rate of inflation.
-- TALKS ON TELECOMS SEEN AS HOPEFUL

The chairman of the World Trade Organisation's talks on global telecoms liberalisation, Neil McMillan, has said that the latest round of negotiations on the issue has been 'extremely encouraging'. McMillan, of Britain's department of trade and industry, said the chances of a successful conclusion being reached by the February 15 deadline had been boosted by the improved offers made by the US and the European Union, and by the apparent desire of other countries to follow this initiative.
-- TELECOM POLICY IS 'DAMAGING MARKET'

London-based consultancy Ovum, an agency which frequently advises governments on regulatory policy, has added its weight to warnings that current regulation of UK telecommunications market could harm competition. The claims were first made by a group of smaller telecoms operators in their 'Open Access Group' study, which identified the main problem as being the 'local loop' - the final connection between telephone exchanges and homes or offices, which at the moment is dominated by British Telecom.
-- BANKS PLAN RUSSIAN TELECOMS MERGER

Under a proposed deal due to be announced later this month, a group of western investment banks will act with the Russian government to combine the country's two largest long-distance telecoms operators. The plan is to merge Rostelcom, currently the dominant national company, with embryonic second carrier Svyazinvest, and then sell 600m stg worth of shares in the new outfit.
-- POWERGEN TO BUY BACK 10 PER CENT OF ITS SHARES

UK electricity generator PowerGen has reported interim results slightly ahead of expectations, with pre-tax profits for the six months to September 30 at 207m stg compared to 133m stg for the same period in 1995. Announcing the results, PowerGen also revealed plans to buy back up to 10 per cent of its shares, a move likely to cost the company about 370m stg.
-- BT SIGNALS DROP IN DEFECTION RATE OF PRIVATE CUSTOMERS TO RIVALS

British Telecom has reported interim pre-tax profits of 1.59bn stg, compared to 1.61bn stg for the same six month period last year. Announcing the results, which were broadly in line with expectations, BT chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield revealed that the rate of defection among the company's residential customers to cable operators and other rivals is showing signs of slowing. Sir Peter said that the number of BT's residential lines has remained stable at 20.5m throughout the year.
-- BNFL SEEKS SMALL RISE IN NUCLEAR DISCHARGE

British-based nuclear fuel reprocessor and waste management company BNFL is to apply to the Environment Agency for a small increase in the permitted amount of radioactivity its Sellafield plant can release into the atmosphere. The request is likely to spark protest from environmentalists, although a pledge to cut low-level emissions to the Irish Sea, expected to accompany the request, will ease tensions with the Irish government which has campaigned vocally on the issue.
